items.title:
How Grok Bot Uses All Apple Services Flawles

A Mac that holds a dedicated Apple Account can become the shared desk where local agents and cloud models exchange reminders, notes, calendar events, and messages through ordinary command-line tools.

The tools talk to the same local databases and frameworks the Apple apps use, so a change made by one process appears for the others through iCloud or a known file path without any custom protocol.

I signed a separate Apple Account into the Mac the agents use. Personal mail, notes, and contacts stay on the main account. The agents write only into the stores that belong to the dedicated account or into local files under a directory they all can reach.

A command-line tool is a small program that accepts a typed instruction and returns a result. On a Mac the place to type it is Terminal. Most of the tools install through Homebrew.

The first run of each tool triggers a macOS permission dialog under System Settings → Privacy & Security. Once the grants are in place, an agent can list today’s reminders, search notes, or send a message by issuing the matching command.

The setup script below can be given to a Grok Bot that already has shell access on the Mac. It checks for Homebrew, installs it if missing, adds the necessary taps, installs the tools, and then runs status or doctor commands that surface the permission prompts.

The bot cannot click the Allow buttons; the user must open System Settings and grant access for Terminal (or the bot’s helper process) to Reminders, Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Messages, Full Disk Access where required, and Automation for the apps that need it. After the grants, the bot re-runs the status checks to confirm.

Grok Bot Prompt:

—

#!/bin/bash
# Grok Bot setup for Apple CLI tools on dedicated account Mac
# Run from Terminal or via bot shell. Approve permission dialogs manually.

set -e

echo "Checking for Homebrew..."
if ! command -v brew >/dev/null 2>&1; then
echo "Installing Homebrew..."
NONINTERACTIVE=1 /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/insta…)"
# Add to PATH for Apple Silicon (adjust if Intel)
if [[ -d /opt/homebrew ]]; then
echo 'eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> ~/.zprofile
eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
fi
else
echo "Homebrew already present."
fi

echo "Updating Homebrew..."
brew update

echo "Installing core tools..."
brew install steipete/tap/remindctl
brew install steipete/tap/imsg
brew tap antoniorodr/memo
brew install antoniorodr/memo/memo
brew install danielhopkins/formulae/apple-tools

echo "Triggering permission checks (approve dialogs in System Settings)..."
remindctl status || true
remindctl authorize || true
imsg chats --limit 1 || true
memo notes --help || true
apple-calendar calendars || true
apple-contacts list || true
apple-mail accounts || true
apple-messages chats || true
apple-phone recents || true
apple-notes search "test" || true

echo "Done. Re-run the status commands after approving permissions."
echo "Example: remindctl today --json"

—-

remindctl uses EventKit to read and write Apple Reminders. It lists items by date or list, adds items with due dates, alarms, recurrence, notes, priorities, and location triggers, and edits, completes, or deletes them. Output is plain text or JSON. An agent that finishes extracting action items from a transcript runs remindctl add "Follow up on budget" --list Shared --due tomorrow --notes "From 11 Oct call". Another agent later runs remindctl list Shared and marks the item complete once the follow-up is logged.
